# How this line differs from `/v2`

This branch is the Go 1.13 line: module `github.com/octoverse-id/octonomy-go`, versions `v1.x`.
`main` is the modern line, module `github.com/octoverse-id/octonomy-go/v2`, where capabilities
originate; this line ports them ([epic #88](https://github.com/octoverse-id/octonomy-go/issues/88)).

**This file is every difference between the two lines' exported APIs, and the reason for each.**
`tools/compatdiff` writes it from two checks, and `make compat-diff` fails when either finds
something this file does not account for:

1. **Parity with `main`**, at [`676486caf50b`](https://github.com/octoverse-id/octonomy-go/tree/676486caf50bbdc0dd9655f09e228e086411f6ca), the commit `tools/compatdiff/baselines.pin`
   names. Every importable package on each side is compared declaration by declaration, by type
   identity rather than spelling: each package's name, constants with their types and values,
   variables, function and method signatures (the method sets of T and of *T), each type's kind
   and comparability, struct fields with their types and struct tags, each interface's whole
   method set, and which of a package's types satisfy its interfaces (593 features on `main` at
   that commit). A difference not listed below fails the check, and so does a listed one that no
   longer exists.
2. **Compatibility with this line's published releases.** Every feature each one exported is
   still here, unchanged, and so is the order of each struct's exported fields, so code that
   compiled against it compiles against this line -- except in the ways any minor release may
   break it, an unkeyed struct literal chief among them ([`docs/versioning.md`](docs/versioning.md),
   the MINOR rule). This check has no exceptions:

   - [`v1.0.0`](https://github.com/octoverse-id/octonomy-go/tree/v1.0.0) (`ad3ced172994`): 150 features.
   - [`v1.1.0`](https://github.com/octoverse-id/octonomy-go/tree/v1.1.0) (`483ad84659b7`): 467 features.

Not compared: each line's module path and the value of `Version`, which name the line rather
than describe it; parameter and type-parameter names (a type parameter prints by position,
`$0`); unexported declarations; and behaviour that changes no declaration. A
difference of that last kind appears below as prose with no features under it, and no check
holds it true -- it is as current as the pull request that last edited it.

## Deliberate differences

### 1. No webhook receiver

This line has no `webhook` package, and that is policy rather than a porting gap: a consumer
that needs a webhook receiver moves to the `/v2` module ([`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md)). The
receiver's typed event payloads are built from `/v2`'s generic optional field type, which this
line does not have (the next section).

Only on `main`:

```text
package webhook
```

### 2. A PATCH cannot clear a nullable field

Every field of a `*Update` struct here is a pointer, or `Metadata`, tagged `omitempty` -- the
shape this line's first release published. On `main` each is `Optional`, a generic type with a
third state, tagged `omitzero`; Go 1.13 has neither type parameters nor that tag option.
Changing a published field's type breaks every caller that sets the field, and this line can
never publish a major to carry a break, so the pointers stay ([`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md),
*Porting from `main`*).

A nil pointer means "leave it alone" and a non-nil one "set it"; neither says "clear it". So
on this line a PATCH cannot set `TagUpdate.ParentID`, `TagUpdate.VocabularyID`,
`TagUpdate.Description` or `VocabularyUpdate.Description` to null
([#64](https://github.com/octoverse-id/octonomy-go/issues/64)). A consumer that must clear one
moves to `/v2`.

The three `MarshalJSON` methods are this line's half of the same decision. With `Metadata`
left a plain map under `omitempty`, `Metadata{}` would be dropped from the body, and they are
what still sends it as `{}`, emptying the stored object
([#37](https://github.com/octoverse-id/octonomy-go/issues/37)).

Only on `main`:

### 3. `Config.APIVersion` defaults to `/api/v1`

`DefaultAPIVersion` is `APIV1` here and `APIV2` on `main`, and `New` selects it when
`Config.APIVersion` is empty. This line's first release sent every request to `/api/v1`, and
moving an existing caller's requests to another surface on an in-range upgrade is a break with
no version to carry it. So `/api/v2`, and the namespace axis with it, is opt-in here: set
`Config.APIVersion` to `octonomy.APIV2`.

Only on `main`:

```text
const DefaultAPIVersion APIVersion = "v2"
```

Only on this line:

```text
const DefaultAPIVersion APIVersion = "v1"
```

### 4. JSON depth guards that only Go 1.13 needs

Go 1.13's `encoding/json` has no cycle detection when it encodes and no depth limit when it
decodes: a `Metadata` that contains itself hangs the process, and a response nested deeply
enough exhausts the stack, which is a fatal runtime error rather than a panic. This line refuses
both before `encoding/json` sees them -- a request body whose Go values (maps, slices, structs,
pointers) nest past 10,000 levels, a cycle among them included, and a response nested past
10,000 levels ([`jsondepth.go`](jsondepth.go),
[#91](https://github.com/octoverse-id/octonomy-go/issues/91)). A modern standard library refuses
a cycle and an over-deep response itself, so `main` carries no such guard; on either line each
of those is an error, and what differs is the code that refuses it and the message it returns.

Two requests differ in outcome. A request body whose Go values nest past 10,000 levels WITHOUT
a cycle is refused here and sent by `main`: a modern encoder detects cycles but sets no depth
limit on the values it encodes. And a `json.RawMessage` in a request body is the caller's own
bytes: the guard does not enter it, and Go 1.13's encoder copies it without recursing, so one
nested past 10,000 levels is sent from this line, where a modern encoder refuses it.

No declaration differs.

## The irreducible type-name delta

### Type parameters, spelled per type

Go 1.13 has no type parameters, so each of `main`'s generic declarations is written here for
the types it is used with.

- `main`'s `List[T]` is one list envelope per resource here -- `TagList`, `VocabularyList`,
  `TagAliasList`, `AuditLogList`, `ResourceTagList` and `TagResourceList` -- each with the same
  `Data` and `Pagination` fields, and every `List` method returns its own resource's envelope.
- `Each` walks a `Page`, an interface every list envelope here implements through its pointer,
  and hands its callback each row as an `interface{}` holding the row's value.
- `DecodeMetadata` takes a pointer to decode into rather than a type argument, as
  `json.Unmarshal` does.

Only on `main`:
